The corpus search resolves cleanly. One document is squarely on-topic for all three terms — *genus*, *surfaces*, and *topology* — and two others touch the theme from adjacent mathematical angles.

## Primary answer: dynamical systems on genus‑*p* surfaces and knot topology

**Document: `0706.2397.pdf` — "Inversely Unstable Solutions of Two‑Dimensional Systems on Genus‑*p* Surfaces and the Topology of Knotted Attractors"** (p. 1)

This paper is entirely about the topology of dynamical systems defined on surfaces of arbitrary genus. Its findings:

- **Setup and goal.** It studies 2‑dimensional (periodic, time‑varying oscillator) systems living on a genus‑*p* surface, generalizing Martins (2004). The central claim is that multiple attractors can coexist and be *linked* on a higher‑genus surface, and that an "inversely unstable solution" forces the relevant invariant set to *not* be homeomorphic to a circle (p. 2).

- **Counting attractors by genus (the topological result).** By induction: on a torus (genus 1) the attractor is a band; on a 2‑hole torus (genus 2) there can be at most 3 attractors; adding one unit of genus introduces another handle giving at most two more attractors — so a genus‑*p* surface carries at most **2*p* − 1** invariant sets (p. 11). Equivalently, a dissipative system on a genus‑*p* surface can have at most *p* topologically distinct knotted attractors (p. 14).

- **Cutting/surgery topology.** Cutting a 2‑hole torus along a knotted trajectory turns the surface topologically into a torus with 2 boundary circles (p. 10). More generally, any system on a genus‑*p* 2‑manifold can be represented on a sphere by cutting each handle along a fundamental circuit containing no equilibrium and filling in the dynamics; conversely one builds higher‑genus systems by surgery on spherical ones (gluing in a dissipative region, cutting the attractor, twisting, and re‑identifying the ends to form a knot) (p. 14).

- **Hyperbolic‑geometry construction.** The most general C^∞ systems on genus‑*p* surfaces are generated from a fundamental domain in the upper‑half‑plane (hyperbolic) model, using automorphic functions invariant under fractional linear transforms; inversely unstable periodic motions become knots on the surface (p. 4).

- **Equilibria are forced by topology.** Via the Poincaré index theorem, any dynamical system on a surface of genus *p* > 1 must have at least one equilibrium point (p. 6).

- **Conclusion.** For a genus‑*p* surface with one unstable cycle, the number of invariant sets may vary but cannot exceed 2*p* − 1; for genus > 1, an individual attractor is not homeomorphic to a circle if it contains an inversely unstable solution (p. 19).

## Secondary / adjacent documents

- **`0706.0028.pdf` — "Py–Calabi quasi‑morphisms and quasi‑states on orientable surfaces of higher genus"** (p. 1). Also concerns higher‑genus surfaces, but from symplectic topology: it works on a closed oriented surface of genus *g* ≥ 2 with a symplectic form, using Reeb graphs and the C²‑topology on C^∞(M) (pp. 6, 9, 12, 32). Relevant to "genus surfaces" but the "topology" here is functional/symplectic rather than the topology of attractors.

- **`0709.2857.pdf` — on Chern numbers of compact complex surfaces** (p. 2: "If two compact complex surfaces are diffeomorphic, then their Chern numbers coincide"). Uses "surfaces," "genus" (Todd genus) and "topological Euler characteristic" (p. 3), but "surface" means a complex algebraic surface, so it matches the keywords only loosely.

## Bottom line

The direct, complete answer to "genus surfaces topology" is **`0706.2397.pdf`**: dynamical systems on genus‑*p* surfaces admit at most **2*p* − 1** invariant sets / **at most *p*** distinct knotted attractors (pp. 11, 14, 19), built via handle‑cutting/surgery and hyperbolic automorphic functions (pp. 4, 10, 14), with equilibria forced by the Poincaré index theorem for genus > 1 (p. 6). `0706.0028.pdf` (higher‑genus symplectic surfaces) and `0709.2857.pdf` (complex‑surface Chern numbers) are thematically adjacent but not the core match.
